rows: Manual handling includes lifting, lowering, pushing, pulling, carrying or otherwise moving a load by hand or bodily force.
Employers should avoid hazardous manual handling so far as reasonably practicable.
Manual-handling operations that cannot be avoided must be assessed for injury risk.
Residual manual-handling risk should be reduced as low as reasonably practicable.
Mechanical aids such as conveyors, pallet trucks or hoists can remove or reduce hazardous handling.
Controls can include reducing load size, carrying distance, twisting and lifting above shoulder height.
Work rate, deadlines, floor condition, lighting, space and temperature can materially affect handling risk.
Good lifting technique supplements, but does not replace, task redesign and mechanical controls.
HSE does not prescribe one universal safe weight limit for every person and task.
A property address alone cannot establish the actual load, frequency, posture, worker capability or handling controls.
Employers must protect workers from health risks arising from regular display-screen equipment use.
The DSE Regulations generally cover workers using screens daily for continuous periods of an hour or more.
Employers must assess DSE workstations and reduce identified risks.
Work routines should include breaks or changes of activity from prolonged screen work.
Employers must arrange an eye test for a DSE user who asks for one.
Glasses must be provided where they are needed only for DSE work.
DSE duties can apply to permanent home workers and workers who routinely split time between home and workplace.
Training should cover workstation adjustment, posture and safe use of display-screen equipment.
DSE use can cause temporary discomfort or fatigue but an address does not prove that a workstation is poorly configured.
Applicability depends on duration, frequency, equipment, workstation setup and the individual worker's circumstances.
Employers must provide required workplace PPE free of charge when a risk assessment shows it is needed.
PPE should be used after risks have been avoided or adequately controlled by other measures where practicable.
PPE must be assessed before use to ensure it is fit for purpose.
Employers must maintain and store PPE properly.
Workers need information, instruction and training on correct PPE use.
PPE selection must match the hazard, wearer, task and working environment.
Emergency PPE needs careful selection, maintenance and regular user training.
Workplace PPE supply must comply with relevant product-safety legislation.
PPE is a residual-risk control and does not by itself prove that the underlying hazard has been adequately managed.
Suitability cannot be inferred from premises type because fit, compatibility, condition and task requirements vary.
LOLER places duties on people and organisations that own, operate or control lifting equipment.
Lifting operations must be properly planned by a competent person.
Lifting operations must be appropriately supervised and carried out safely.
Lifting equipment must be fit for purpose and appropriate for the task.
Equipment used for lifting must be suitably marked.
Many items of lifting equipment require periodic thorough examination.
Records must be kept of thorough examinations.
Specified defects must be reported to the responsible person and, where required, the enforcing authority.
Whether LOLER applies depends on the equipment and activity, not merely the existence of a workplace.
A parcel or building record cannot verify planning quality, competence, examination status or equipment condition.
